title: Using standard algebraic identities
summary: Recognise three standard identities, use them for expansion and factorisation, and apply them to efficient numerical and algebraic reasoning.
objectives: Recall and distinguish the two perfect-square identities and the difference-of-squares identity.
Apply identities to expand, factorise and simplify expressions.
Use identities for efficient exact calculations and verification.

sections.title: Perfect squares contain a middle term

blocks.text: Squaring a binomial means multiplying the complete binomial by itself. The middle term appears twice, so (a+b)² is a²+2ab+b². With subtraction, the middle term is negative but both square terms remain positive.

A common error is to write (a+b)²=a²+b². This omits 2ab. To recognise a perfect-square trinomial, check that the first and last terms are squares and that the middle term is twice the product of their square roots.

sections.title: Difference of squares has conjugate factors

blocks.text: The expression a²-b² factorises because the middle terms cancel when (a+b)(a-b) is expanded. The operation must be subtraction; a sum of two squares does not factorise this way over the real numbers.
Look beyond single letters. For example, 9x²-25 is (3x)²-5², so its factors are (3x+5)(3x-5). Remove any common factor first, then check whether the remaining expression is a difference of squares.

The identities work in both directions. They can expand a compact product, factorise a polynomial, simplify an expression or calculate numbers near a convenient base. For 103×97, view the factors as (100+3)(100-3).

Verification is built in: expand proposed factors and compare every coefficient with the original expression. For numerical calculations, estimate first so that a missing square or incorrect sign is obvious.
